title: Metta, revisited
hookLine: kindness wishes well; its near enemy is clinging affection (Visuddhimagga 9)
last: BRAHMAVIHARA — BOUNDLESS AND FREE OF HATRED.

cards: Some love feels like a gift, and some feels like a grip. The friend who's glad when good things happen to you, even when it means you move away.
And the one whose affection comes with strings: text me back, need me, don't change. Both call it love. Both might even feel warm from the inside.
But one leaves you free and the other doesn't. A Buddhist manual written fifteen hundred years ago drew exactly this line.

teach.b: You met metta in camp three: kindness, loving-kindness, from mitta, a friend. The phrases, the benefactor, the difficult person, the six directions.

Now i want to go deeper, with the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, a great manual of meditation written in Sri Lanka by the monk Buddhaghosa in the fifth century. Its ninth chapter maps each of the four rooms.
Metta's mark, it says, is promoting the welfare of others. Its job is to prefer their welfare. It shows up as the melting away of ill will.

Then the surprise: every room has two enemies. The far enemy is the obvious opposite, easy to spot. The near enemy is sneakier: it looks like the real thing, feels like it, and quietly takes its place.
For metta, the near enemy is greed, clinging affection, attachment that wants something back. It's near, the manual explains, because both kindness and clinging notice what's good in a person.

teach.h: MAY YOU BE WELL, NOT MAY YOU BE MINE.
teach.b: One says, may you be well. The other says, may you be mine. So metta succeeds when it makes ill will fade, and fails when it turns into sticky, selfish affection.
That's why the manual suggests starting not with a romantic partner, where the line blurs easily, but with yourself, and then a benefactor, someone who has helped you, like a teacher.
None of this means affection is wrong. Families and friendships run on it.
The point is to know the difference from the inside: kindness wishes well, and lets go.

how: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions teach the near and far enemies from the Visuddhimagga, so students can tell real kindness from its look-alikes; metta practice often begins with oneself or a benefactor rather than a romantic partner.

o: a calm feeling of peace that comes in meditation
kindness that wishes others well and lets go
warm affection that holds on to the ones you love

games.q: match each piece of the manual's map of metta.

s: the Visuddhimagga says affection is always wrong
it warns that metta fails when it turns into sticky, selfish affection; families and friendships run on affection.
the near enemy is dangerous because it looks like the real thing
both kindness and clinging notice what's good in a person.
the manual was written in Sri Lanka in the fifth century

games.q: a friend is moving across the country for a job they've wanted for years. you'll miss them. what does metta sound like here?
o: 'may you be well, and thrive there.'
say nothing and hope it falls through.
games.why: the manual's line: kindness says 'may you be well'; its near enemy, clinging, says 'may you be mine'.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love and offer the old wish silently: may you be well, may you be happy.
Then look gently underneath it for a string, a wanting them to stay, to need you, to turn out a certain way, and if you find one, just see it, without scolding yourself.
Then wish again with the string cut: may you be well, however your life turns out.

wordCard.voice: Metta. Kindness that wishes others well; its near enemy is clinging affection, which looks warm but wants something back.

orig.note: Pali mettā: kindness, loving-kindness, from mitta, a friend.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness, not clinging. The first room, with its look-alike at the door. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (metta: characteristic, function, near and far enemies)
